title: Full Failure Profile of the Ordinary-Derivative Multiplicity Test over 𝔽_q
description: Over a characteristic-zero field, (X − a)ᵏ ∣ p iff p and its first k − 1 ordinary derivatives vanish at a. In positive characteristic this test fails — the sibling entry factor-remainder-theorem-oq-01-oq-02 repairs it with Hasse derivatives and records a single witness (derivative(X²) = 0 over ZMod 2). This entry pins down the FULL failure profile over an arbitrary characteristic-p field (hence every finite field 𝔽_q = 𝔽_{p^f}). Using Mathlib's identity derivative^[k] f = k! • hasseDeriv k f, it proves the exact threshold (k! : F) = 0 ↔ p ≤ k, deduces that the ordinary test is reliable exactly up to order p − 1 and identically blind from order p on, and generalizes the Xᵖ counterexample to the whole family X^{p^e}: the Hasse test returns the true multiplicity p^e while every positive-order ordinary derivative vanishes, overcounting without bound. 15 theorems, 0 axioms, 0 sorries.

originalContributions: factorial_cast_eq_zero_iff: the EXACT threshold — over a characteristic-p ring, (k! : F) = 0 ↔ p ≤ k. This single biconditional governs the entire failure profile, since the ordinary derivative is the Hasse derivative scaled by k!.

iterate_derivative_eq_smul_hasseDeriv: the scaling identity in base-field-scalar form, derivative^[k] f = (k! : F) • hasseDeriv k f, repackaging Mathlib's factorial_smul_hasseDeriv with the scalar pushed into F.

iterate_derivative_eq_zero_of_char_le: above the threshold the ordinary test is BLIND — for p ≤ k, derivative^[k] f = 0 for every polynomial f, so ordinary derivatives carry no multiplicity information at orders ≥ p.

iterate_derivative_eq_zero_iff_hasseDeriv_of_lt: below the threshold the two tests AGREE — for k < p over a field, derivative^[k] f = 0 ↔ hasseDeriv k f = 0, since (k! : F) is then a unit. Together with the previous result this localizes reliability exactly to orders 0..p−1.

failure_profile_X_pow: the full family generalization — over any field of characteristic p with e ≥ 1, rootMultiplicity 0 (X^{p^e}) = p^e (the Hasse-recoverable truth) while every positive-order ordinary derivative of X^{p^e} vanishes, so the ordinary test certifies multiplicity ≥ k at 0 for every k, overcounting the true value p^e without bound — generalizing the Xᵖ / 𝔽_p witness to all X^{p^e}.

overview.historicalContext: The multiplicity form of the Factor Theorem says, over a field of characteristic zero, that (X − a)ᵏ ∣ p iff p and its first k − 1 ordinary derivatives p^{(j)} = derivative^[j] p vanish at a — the statement that the Taylor expansion of p at a begins at order k. In positive characteristic the criterion breaks: over ZMod p, derivative(Xᵖ) = 0, so the ordinary derivatives can all vanish while the multiplicity is large. Helmut Hasse's divided-power derivative hasseDeriv repairs the criterion by avoiding division by m!, and Mathlib records the repair plus a single witness of the breakdown. The natural follow-up question is quantitative: at exactly which derivative order does the ordinary test go blind, and how badly does it misreport multiplicities? This entry answers both over an arbitrary characteristic-p field (hence over every finite field 𝔽_q).
overview.problemStatement: Over a field of characteristic p (every 𝔽_q = 𝔽_{p^f}), determine the exact order at which the ordinary iterated-derivative multiplicity test fails, and exhibit the full family of counterexamples. Concretely: prove (k! : F) = 0 ↔ p ≤ k; deduce that derivative^[k] f = 0 for all f when p ≤ k (blind) and that derivative^[k] f = 0 ↔ hasseDeriv k f = 0 when k < p (reliable); and show that for X^{p^e} (e ≥ 1) the true multiplicity at 0 is p^e while every positive-order ordinary derivative vanishes.
overview.proofStrategy: Everything hinges on Mathlib's factorial_smul_hasseDeriv: derivative^[k] f = k! • hasseDeriv k f. Pushing the scalar into the base field gives derivative^[k] f = (k! : F) • hasseDeriv k f, so the ordinary derivative loses information exactly when (k! : F) vanishes. Part I computes that vanishing precisely: CharP.cast_eq_zero_iff turns (k! : F) = 0 into p ∣ k!, and Nat.Prime.dvd_factorial turns p ∣ k! into p ≤ k. Part II reads off the two regimes: for p ≤ k the scalar is 0, so derivative^[k] f = 0 for all f (zero_smul); for k < p the scalar is a unit (isUnit_iff_ne_zero plus the threshold), so IsUnit.smul_eq_zero makes the ordinary and Hasse derivatives vanish together. Part III instantiates the family X^{p^e}: rootMultiplicity_X_sub_C_pow gives the true multiplicity p^e at 0, while CharP.cast_eq_zero_iff applied to p ∣ p^e kills the first ordinary derivative, and iterating kills every positive-order one.
keyInsights: The ordinary derivative is the Hasse derivative scaled by k!: derivative^[k] f = (k! : F) • hasseDeriv k f. So all failure of the ordinary test is failure of the scalar (k! : F), nothing more.
The threshold is razor-sharp: (k! : F) = 0 ↔ p ≤ k. The ordinary test is therefore reliable at orders 0,1,…,p−1 and identically blind at every order ≥ p — a clean cutoff, not a gradual decay.
Below the cutoff the ordinary and Hasse tests are literally equivalent (the scalar is a unit); the divided-power refinement only adds information at orders ≥ p.

The X^{p^e} family makes the failure maximal: the Hasse test returns the exact multiplicity p^e, yet every positive-order ordinary derivative is identically zero, so the naive test would certify arbitrarily high multiplicity at 0 — unbounded overcounting.
Because every finite field 𝔽_q has characteristic p, the whole profile applies verbatim to all of 𝔽_q, not just the prime field 𝔽_p.

sections.title: Overview: full failure profile of the ordinary-derivative multiplicity test over 𝔽_q
sections.summary: The polynomial/char-p imports (HasseDeriv, Derivative, RingDivision, Taylor, Div, CharP.Basic, Prime.Factorial, Tactic) and the module docstring. Pins down exactly at which derivative order the ordinary iterated-derivative multiplicity test goes blind over a characteristic-p field (hence every 𝔽_q = p^f), and generalizes the Xᵖ/𝔽_p counterexample to the whole family X^{p^e}.
sections.mathContext: The engine is Mathlib's factorial_smul_hasseDeriv: derivative^[k] f = k!•hasseDeriv k f, so the ordinary derivative is the Hasse derivative scaled by k!, and information loss is governed entirely by whether (k! : F) vanishes. Main results: factorial_cast_eq_zero_iff (the exact threshold (k!:F) = 0 ↔ p ≤ k, via Nat.Prime.dvd_factorial); iterate_derivative_eq_smul_hasseDeriv (scaling identity); iterate_derivative_eq_zero_of_char_le (above the threshold every ordinary derivative vanishes — blind at orders ≥ p); iterate_derivative_eq_zero_iff_hasseDeriv_of_lt (below the threshold the two agree, k! a unit) — together the ordinary test is reliable exactly up to order p−1 and useless from order p on. The concrete X^{p^e} family (rootMultiplicity_X_pow, derivative_X_pow_char, iterate_derivative_X_pow_char_eq_zero, failure_profile_X_pow) shows the Hasse test returns the true multiplicity p^e while every positive-order ordinary derivative vanishes. Part IV proves the positive complement — the Hasse-derivative multiplicity criterion sub_pow_dvd_iff_hasseDeriv_eval_eq_zero over any commutative ring.

conclusion.summary: A fully verified (0 sorries, 0 axioms, no native_decide) file of 280 lines and 15 theorems giving the complete failure profile of the ordinary-derivative multiplicity test over an arbitrary characteristic-p field (every 𝔽_q). The exact threshold (k! : F) = 0 ↔ p ≤ k splits the order axis cleanly: the ordinary test is reliable (equivalent to the Hasse test) exactly at orders 0..p−1 and identically blind at every order ≥ p. The X^{p^e} family realizes the worst case — true multiplicity p^e at 0, yet every positive-order ordinary derivative vanishes, so the naive test overcounts without bound.
conclusion.implications: This quantifies the qualitative breakdown recorded by the sibling Hasse entry: it is not a sporadic failure but a sharp cutoff at order p, uniform across every finite field. The reliable-up-to-(p−1) result justifies using ordinary derivatives for low-order multiplicity in characteristic p, while the blind-from-p result and the X^{p^e} family show exactly where and how badly the Hasse refinement becomes indispensable — e.g. for separability/inseparability detection where polynomials in Xᵖ are precisely the inseparable obstructions.
openQuestions: Quantify the overcounting for a general polynomial: characterize, in terms of its p-adic structure, the gap between the multiplicity certified by the ordinary derivatives and the true (Hasse) multiplicity at a root.
Extend the threshold analysis to mixed characteristic and to the truncated jet algebras F[X]/(X^n), where only finitely many Hasse derivatives are visible.

openQuestions.question: The reliability range m ≤ p is sharp via the single witness X^p at the threshold m = p+1. Characterize the FULL set of (f, a, m) over 𝔽_q for which the ordinary-derivative test mis-certifies multiplicity at order m = p+1 (or general m > p): is it exactly the polynomials with a p-th-power factor (X − a)^p ∣ f vanishing under all ordinary derivatives, and what is the precise gap between the ordinary-certified multiplicity ⌊·⌋ and the true Hasse multiplicity?

sub_pow_dvd_iff_hasseDeriv_eval_eq_zero is a characteristic-free Hasse-derivative multiplicity criterion assembled from Mathlib primitives. Is it worth upstreaming to Mathlib as the divided-power companion of le_rootMultiplicity_iff, and does it give a cleaner derivation of rootMultiplicity via natTrailingDegree (taylor a f)?
